utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The Chamber will first issue its ruling on the accused's request for adjournment to prepare for his testimony filed on the 11th of February, 2014, wherein he seeks a two-week adjournment prior to the start of his testimony and requests that his testimony begins on the 11th of March, 2014. The Prosecution responded on the 12th of February, not opposing this request. Having considered the accused's arguments, the Chamber has decided to granted the request in part and hereby orders that the testimony of the accused shall commence on the 4th of March, 2014. The Chamber takes this opportunity to remind the accused that the Chamber initially granted him 300 hours in which to present his entire defence case, which was augmented to 325 hours after Count 1 was reinstated in the indictment following the appeal judgement on the 11th of July, 2013. On these -- of these 325 hours, as of the end of yesterday's hearing, the accused had used 301 hours and 18 minutes, thereby leaving him with 23 hours and 42 minutes left in which to present the remainder of his case. The Chamber has voiced on repeated occasions that it was concerned with the manner in which the accused chose to spend the time allocated to him and considered that, having passed the 300-hour mark, it was opportune to remind him once again. Next, on the topic of scheduling, Mr. Tieger, the Chamber wished to inquire whether the Prosecution is in a position to state whether it will be minded to file a motion to present rebuttal evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, the Chamber expects you to file that -- file it by 4th of March, 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Robinson, in reference to the Defence submission of evidence related to sentencing filed on the 8th of January, 2014, in which the Defence tenders for admission a number of documents related to the Holbrooke Agreement, my colleagues would like you to file a supplemental submission, elaborating further on how these documents are relevant to sentencing and/or mitigation of sentence. In other words, rather than simply repeating the ruling of the Appeals Chamber on this, you are requested to articulate what your case is on their relevance to sentencing. Could you file this submission by the close of business on Tuesday, next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And just one further thing, I just wanted to put it on record that the Chamber yesterday instructed its Legal Officer to communicate to the parties as to the redaction of certain paragraphs of statements of Mr. Sarac and Glamocic. Unless there's further thing to be discussed, we'll bring in the next witness. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. On the subject of scheduling, I just wanted to advise the Chamber that, as you've instructed, we have waited until the end of our case before making bar table motions, but we will be making some. So if you wish to set any dead-lines for those, it would be helpful to know those as far in advance as possible, but we will be working on those as we go along and after the testimony of Dr. Karadzic concludes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will come back to this issue. Thank you. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jurisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue with your cross-examination. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jurisic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, in your written evidence you, I noted, said that while the Muslims in Kljuc were being mopped up and disarmed by the police and the army, there were some renegades who you said were out of control, who were killing them at Velagici and plundering their homes and destroying their property. And I want to ask you about that. But I want to talk first about Velagici. Actually, you know who the perpetrators are of the massacre at Velagici, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day after this happened at Velagici, I found out in the office of the president of the municipality, I heard the officers talking about a crime that had been committed. I didn't know what had happened at the time. However, when I heard that the military police would go and arrest someone, later on it became apparent that the military police identified two or three rogue soldiers who committed the crime. I know that the investigating judge drafted a record and that the military police took these two into custody in the Banja Luka detention facility. They were subsequently released - I don't know how this came about - into the 7th Kupres Motorised Brigade and they stayed in that brigade. This was the extent of my knowledge. I only came to learn more of these details later. I didn't know the real truth at the time. What I do know is that the four of them were investigated and interviewed and detained in the military remand prison in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also know, as you've just said, they were released, they were never prosecuted; right? They weren't prosecuted until after the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were released and assigned to the 7th Kupres Brigade. It was only based on some reports and records that I saw that they were there and that they stayed there until the end of the war, although they were re-assigned to other units. However, they were not detained or tried after that first instance when they were taken into custody in the Banja Luka prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, did you say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies, in line 18, I'd like to know where this comes from, what's the reference for the fact that they were never prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She asked -- she supplemented, they weren't prosecuted until after the end of the war. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a look, please, at P3616.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, there's a difference. It's not true that they were not prosecuted. If -- they may not have been put at trial until the end of the war, but it's not that a decision was made not to prosecute them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is beyond the intervention for the purpose of cross-examination. The witness sufficiently understood the question. I think we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, this document is from the military prosecutor's office at the 1st Krajina Corps command, and it's dated 29 July 1993. And this is the document -- and this document says that proceedings against the suspects began in 1993 but were terminated. And the very last sentence of the largest paragraph says that one of the reasons they were terminated is "because of the stance of the deputy prime minister of the Republika Srpska and the chairman of the Kljuc Municipality Executive Committee ..." So, Mr. Jurisic, this document shows that the prosecutions -- that the municipal authorities of your municipality were making sure those prosecutions never happened; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm for you that I didn't hear anything about this from any of the official organs. After this happened, no meetings were convened or anything of the sort. These were stories that circulated in the municipality. I cannot claim that somebody was directly in favour of this. I can only tell you that those of us municipal officials were not aware of the fact that their release was being sought. I don't know how anyone from the Executive Board could have -- we didn't even have a president of the Executive Board. We only have -- had a vice-president who was acting president. He was the vice-president to the previous president who wasn't there anymore. I don't know if anybody talked to the military. I can't deny it or confirm it. I know that they were released, and that's the only thing I know. I don't know what followed. I know that the perpetrators stayed within the Kupres Brigade until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody informed us of the fact that there had been an intervention to release them. My general impression of the whole affair was that the municipal authorities and others, when it came to these individuals who meted out their own justice, wanted to have them isolated because they were a threat to the citizens of Kljuc no matter what their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on then, given what you've just said about the municipal authorities. Mr. Jurisic, we've got the log-books for the Kljuc basic prosecutor's office from 1992 right through to 1995. And I'm going to call them up, they're 65 ter number 26009, and we're going to have to go to Sanction to have a look at these. And if you want to see a paper copy, I can give you one, but the handwriting is pretty small and you might need some kind of magnification, but I've got one for you if you like. Now, what you've got in front of you, Mr. Jurisic, is the log-book for 1992 and we're going to look, first of all, at pages -- page 5 of this log-book which covers entries from 27 May to the 1st of June of 1992. And I've had a detailed look at this. First of all, Mr. Jurisic, there's no criminal report submitted between the 1st of May and the 30th of June, so I just want to show you the type of thing that did get submitted. I want to go to entry number 50, it's about halfway down the page and that shows that there was a criminal report filed against a Serb by the name of Milan Radakovic for violation of Article 129 of the criminal code in force. And I had a look at what that is, that is illicit commerce. Let's go down to entry 51, that's the 30th of June, that's a criminal report against two Serbs for aggravated theft. And we'll go down to 52, 53, and 54 in succession. The next one dated June 30th is a criminal report against a Muslim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I'm not sure the witness can follow. Can he read this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could magnify it, but it becomes -- the image becomes pixelated, but I could absolutely give him the hard copy that I have beside me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Defence have a hard copy as well so that we may follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope Mr. Sladojevic could teach you how to upload in your e-court. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we were at entry number 52, it's a report of an allegation of fraud against a Muslim passing a bad cheque, I think. Entry number 53, that's another violation against a Muslim for fraud dated June 30th. And the final one, entry 54, also June 30th, is a violation against a Serb individual for grave offences against the safety of public transport. And then when you've had a chance to look at that I want to go over to the next page. I want to go over to entry 57 on the next page, which is page 7 of 65 ter number 26009. And there you see an entry dated 16 July 1992 against a Muslim for a murder that happened in April of that year and he sentenced to 20 years in jail. And entry number 63, dated September 4th, shows a report against two Muslims for destruction of prominent production facilities, in this case something belonging to Banja Luka TV. And in November they were sentenced eventually to seven years in prison. There were no criminal reports in this book submitted also around the 10th of July, 1992. In fact, there's not a single criminal report in this log-book that shows anyone was ever prosecuted in Kljuc for the looting or the arson or the killings you discussed. No one was ever brought to court. Now, my question to you is: Being in the function that you were, meeting with the people that you did - and we talked about those at the beginning of your testimony yesterday - being present at Municipal Assembly meetings throughout the course of the war, you would know that, wouldn't you? You'd be able to confirm this, no one was ever prosecuted for the torching, for the destruction, for the arson, for the killings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any direct influence to wield in this, nor was I able to follow from this register you've shown to me. I only know one person, Radenko Kuburic, I don't know under which number I saw him, under 54, page 1. Page 1, number 54. As for the others against whom criminal reports were filed, I can tell that all of them were Muslims. In what way the prosecutor worked and what sort of offences were committed, well, obviously there was arson and looting by these rogue groups. I don't know what was within the police's power to do. The only thing I can conclude from this is that reports were filed against one side only and that's the Muslim side. It's very difficult for me to speak about the specific case because I really don't have any knowledge about the people or the offences committed. This was within the purview of the police to attend the scenes. I wasn't able to follow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. The system was working, though, wasn't it? That's what this also shows. The prosecutor's office was working.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the prosecutor's office was working, but it all depends - well, the way I see it - how the police worked, how many crimes did they uncover, how could they sanction this legally.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's get back to the original question I asked you which you didn't answer. You can confirm that there were no prosecutions for the arsons, the destructions, the looting, and the killing that you talked about. You would know that because of your position in the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only hear of individual things, things that were done by individuals, but I did not receive any reports from the ground because that was not within my domain of work, all of these things that were happening. Because as far as I know, what was always insisted upon was that these perpetrators should be prosecuted and punished. Now, what the prosecutor's office did was completely apart from my line of work. Only when there were some characteristic cases, when there were reports from the police, if it was something big. But I really cannot give a precise answer to this. I cannot say. Because there were such cases all over, so I didn't even know all these perpetrators so I cannot have a relevant opinion in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just, please, Mr. Jurisic. I try not to interrupt you. Please don't interrupt me. I really do try not to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 26009 as a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours, and what I would propose to do is translate the entries that we've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I don't believe that this witness is a proper witness who can lay a foundation for this document. He's had nothing to do with the courts or the police, and as we saw yesterday with the witness, without giving much detail in public session, documents shown by Dr. Karadzic appeared which were not shown on a log like this. So it's not -- we don't believe it's proper for the Prosecution to produce this kind of document with this witness who has no connection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the connection is not really an authentication issue, which isn't an issue here. The real issue or the reason why this is relevant and being tendered is that not only is the witness being impeached by it, but in fact, Your Honours, the witness confirmed he recognised the name of one of the individuals who was listed on this document, made comments about what the document shows, and specifically recalled or, pardon me, generally recalled some of the circumstances of the handling of these cases from his involvement in the municipal organs of that time. I think he's established an excellent foundation for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the witness is not in a position to make any comments on these items except the one he identified, i.e., Radenko Kuburic. So we'll admit that part, but otherwise we'll not admit the others. We'll assign a number being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour that will be MFI P6671.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And further, your purpose of impeachment has been accomplished by putting the questions to the witness and hearing the witness's answer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jurisic, you talked about the intentions of the municipal authorities in one of your answers to me, saying that you and the municipal authorities insisted that the perpetrator should be prosecuted and punished. And I'd like to show you in that regard another document, 1D -- pardon me, D1738. Now, this, Mr. Jurisic, is a report to the 1 KK command dated 16 February 1993 on the situation in Kljuc, and it's based on a meeting that you attended along with Mr. Banjac and Mr. Kondic and Mr. Kalabic. And I'd like to go over to page 2 in both languages of this document, and in B/C/S I think the paragraph is -- the relevant paragraph, you'll find it at the second-to-last full paragraph from the bottom. It says, talking about the events at the onset of the war, it says: "Individuals and small and large groups of people began illegally appropriating Muslim property in Muslim villages and hamlets during combat operations in the local communes of Velagici, Sanica, Humici, and Peci, and continued to do so when operations ended. This was done by military personnel, members of the police, and local Serbs ..." So what this document shows is that everybody knew who was doing it; right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the police organs and the military security organs that were in that area could identify those perpetrators. I don't know to what extent this would have -- well, according to this report and some of the things that I managed to hear in Kljuc from the people there, such things did happen, yes, they did happen. Now, did the army do that? I think the army had other tasks, the police too. However, certain individuals, renegades, took every opportunity to get into that area that was not covered and probably there was some looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's go down further in this document to page 3, the second paragraph -- actually, the fifth paragraph on page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, actually, we'll start at the second paragraph. This says, Mr. Jurisic -- this talks about the incidents that we're discussing -- second full paragraph, pardon me. This mentions that, apart from issuing a decision taking appropriated property on to the state and into the state coffers, it says: Nothing was done to prevent further acts of unlawful appropriation of the property which had been proclaimed as state owned. And then if we skip down to paragraph number 5, it talks about people driving luxury cars and tractors and trailers, and the last sentence of paragraph 5 says: "These and other acts are being committed in full view of those who are supposed to stop and prevent them and this in full co-ordinated action and co-operation of the military and civilian police." So the fact is, Mr. Jurisic, completely contrary to what you say, people were looting and pillaging in a climate of complete impunity and there was no intention on the part of Kljuc municipal authorities to punish anyone because even by February 1993 it was happening under your nose and you weren't doing anything about it. That's what was actually going on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that at all meetings, starting from the Crisis Staff and the Executive Board and so on, that what was always insisted upon was that police was supposed to provide protection for 24 hours a day, around-the-clock, for the Muslim and Croatian population. At first there was some very good results achieved there for as long as the police could do it around-the-clock. I remember at Biljansko Polje immediately when the operation started - and this was rather characteristic so I remember the name - Bogdan Skrbic was killed during the night during a looting, but the police complained and said that it was very hard to prevent. And I did not deny that this kind of thing did happen, but I claim that in spite of all these efforts made to have the police and army prevent the looting of property this did happen nevertheless. Now, how many measures were taken against these people, I cannot say. I know that there was looted property that was then taken back on roads, but obviously all of this could not have been prevented. I'm absolutely not denying that this kind of thing did happen. I'm not denying that that happened. To what extent and who fared how, I really have no insight. I heard this information briefly at meetings, and the police probably knew what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just ask you -- before I ask you one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm approaching my time, which I understood to be an hour and a half. And I feel I may, although I'm usually quite diligent, leak over that by about another ten minutes and I just wanted to foreshadow that with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has no difficulty with it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, you were a member of an organ that you said yourself yesterday was the highest organ of authority in the municipality. It would have been the simplest thing for you to ensure the rule of law was enforced in Kljuc and the Crisis Staff didn't do that, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attempts to do that and to have public law and order did exist, and that was done very responsibly but it could not have been carried through completely. In Kljuc there were soldiers and all sorts of people that nobody knew. They came from all sorts of places and to place them all under control, that was very difficult. It would have suited us in Kljuc the best to have public law and order, but often things did not happen the way we would have wanted them to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said now in your written evidence that you never heard anyone order, plan, or investigate -- or, pardon me, instigate the expulsion of non-Serbs from Kljuc. And I actually want to show you a different document now in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: P2641. That's not it. Let me check the number that I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is 4621 but you said 264.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm in complete sympathy. Transposing numbers is something I do myself more often than I like.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Jurisic, is conclusions from a subregional meeting of political representatives of municipalities -- the Serbian municipalities of Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc, your municipality, and it's dated 7 June 1992. I'd like us to go over to paragraph 6, please, and that's on page 2 in both languages. Paragraph 6 reads that: "All seven municipalities," the ones that I've just named, in their "subregion agree that Muslims and Croats should move out ... until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities ..." That's a plan to move non-Serbs from Kljuc, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this at all. This is the first time that I see this. I'm not a member of any of that. I was not present anywhere. Nobody showed us anything, and I claim with full responsibility that this is the first time I see all of this. Who took part in this, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. That actually doesn't answer my question, but I'll ask you -- I'll move on. So I'm a bit surprised because it was your job as Secretary of National Defence to approve the departure of people from Kljuc. And you're saying you don't know anything about this document or this plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of anyone adopting such a plan. I had no opportunity of seeing that or being present, especially this meeting, some region. I never had the opportunity of attending any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, now since it was your job to approve departure, I want to ask you a couple more questions. Your evidence is that -- or actually, when we finished off yesterday in your testimony in chief you talked about fear in the population and that's exactly right. Non-Serbs in Kljuc in the summer of 1992 were scared, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Some people had lost their jobs. Some people had been arrested. Some locations -- villages had been attacked. There was rampant crime, in your own words, so that people weren't safe inside their own homes. That would wipe away anybody's sense of safety and security, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I said yesterday and I'm saying today, these are these terrible things that happen in war time, renegades, especially in areas that are outside urban areas that are difficult to control. The police went even during the night to secure these places. It was very hard. All sorts of things happened. It would be unfair to say the people did not live in fear. I can say here with full responsibility that persons who were not non-Serbs also had such problems. There were attacks against people, property, all kinds of revenge. So the situation was highly complex.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's talk about the non-Serbs for a minute. Based on what you've said and what you said in your written evidence, they left because they had no other real choice, did they? Because they had been subject to systematic crimes, they felt they were at risk of crimes, and they could have no confidence that the authorities were going to protect them, that's why they left; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people left primarily for these reasons of safety and security because they saw that there was a war-time situation there, that it was difficult. Also, people were jobless, they could not earn a living, it was very hard to protect one's property. So people found a way out by leaving that territory and finding other places where they could live better. At the time I heard that there was -- well, let me not call it guess-work, but let's say forecasts, namely that people of Muslim ethnicity had received signals from their authorities. That's what people were saying at least, that it would be best to leave all of that until some other conditions were created. I don't know what that was, but it became very massive.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on top of those people who -- those non-Serbs who hadn't been killed and hadn't been arrested and wanted to leave who -- who came to you, they had to get a permit and sign a statement that they were leaving forever to get that permission; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This permit that we gave, that was just keeping records as to who was leaving and also that such persons could have guarantees that they reported to the military organ so that they could cross at all the check-points that they would come across in Republika Srpska. This permit was not only given to ethnic Muslims and ethnic Croats, but also to ethnic Serbs if they would leave the area of the municipality --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we did not have people signing any kind of certificates about handing over property or leaving on a permanent basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're saying, so you're saying, that in order to get a permit to leave, the non-Serbs of Kljuc didn't have to sign any documents; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we're concerned, I claim with full responsibility that they didn't have to sign any documents whatsoever, those stating that they were leaving their property or that they were leaving for good. The only thing I did hear there was, I don't know, at some meetings, that at the Crisis Staff of this ARK Krajina there was some document that arrived from there about handing over property. But people who were trained lawyers and who were well-versed said that that was impossible to carry out because there was very little time. Also, the courts of law couldn't deal with that and just to take one's word for that wouldn't mean a thing. It just needed -- it was just necessary to keep records so that the procedure would be very short and the people could have no problems when going through check-points that were under police control and there were quite a few of those because each and every municipality had them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So based on what you say, can I understand that so long as non-Serbs said that they were leaving forever or giving their property to the municipality, they were allowed to go; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked them, as far as we were concerned, either to hand over their property or to leave on a permanent basis. They wanted to leave. Where they would go, how long they would stay, whatever. As for property, as far as I know, there were possibilities of exchanges. I know that people made these fictitious contracts. They wanted their property to be guarded. I know there were exchanges for houses along the seacoast, Pag and other places. However, the important thing for us was to know whether people were going and whether their property was remaining there so that we could protect it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's just have a look at one document and then I'll close, that's P3462. Right. Mr. Jurisic, this is a decision of the Kljuc War Presidency that you were a member of of 30 July 1992 and this says, under Article 1 that: "... families and persons who issue a statement to the appropriate organ ... declaring that they are moving permanently from the territory of ... the municipality, shall be permitted to leave ..." And if you go on to Article 2, that says if they haven't signed their property over to the municipality or exchanged it with Serbs within three months of leaving, the municipality is going to take it away anyway. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we can go over actually to the second page of the document in both languages. Article -- sorry, we can stay on page 1 in B/C/S -- no, we are on the right page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Article 7 of this document says: "On the basis of a state of voluntary moving ... from the municipality or a legally valid contract," an exchange contract, "the National Defence Secretariat," that's you, "shall grant ... agreement to leave ... Kljuc ..." So this is a contemporaneous document that says exactly what you have just denied to us. People had to sign a statement, non-Serbs had to sign a statement that they were leaving forever and give their property to the municipality. There was nothing voluntary about it, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, as far as we were concerned, we did not ask for any kind of proof about the hand-over of property or anything else. Any citizen who said they wanted to move out would receive this permit in order to be able to cross the check-points. We were not authorised to carry out any kind of signing about the hand-over of somebody's property or an exchange or there was no time-limitation. We would issue permits to move outside of the municipality to Serbs as well who were leaving and going to some other municipality, so that we would know where they were moving. We didn't ask for any certificates, we didn't receive any, I don't know who could have asked for such a certificate. All I'm saying is that if somebody came to the Crisis Staff to ask that, that was so. We just wanted to have a record of all the property so that we would know how many people left so that we could preserve what we could. In more urban areas such as Kljuc and Sanica, this property to a great extent was preserved, but there was no torching or any major destruction of the buildings. There was more destruction of buildings in the rural, village areas. I am repeating this. I cannot say anything else. We -- there was no certificate involved. A person would come, say: I'm going to such and such a place, and we would issue a permit so that he would be free to move. It was up to him what he would do with his house. We just wanted to have a record that he handed over the property or that he was leaving it behind or that he exchanged it, although that was not the topic of our work, regardless of what he wrote. It does not have to -- it doesn't have to mean that the people in the Presidency and in the Crisis Staff knew the regulations very well and were aware of what they had to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And have we just heard your defence to the allegations of forced transfer and deportation that your facing in front of the state court in Bosnia in the investigation against you? Is that your defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not take part in any forcible transfer or in any decisions on that matter. That was not my job by far, and that is something that I would not have wished to have done anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could this document remain in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jurisic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us if you know the signature of the late Jovo Banjac and is this his signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise his signature, but I don't see where you are showing it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the right half of the screen in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you mean this document that we're seeing right now, that the Madam Prosecutor was reading from to me just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm just pausing between question and answer and I kindly ask you that you do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we zoom in. Just the signature part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Banjac's signature and is this it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it a number of times, but this is very indistinct. I cannot really see it very well or it's a bad copy, but from what I can see this is not his. I've already seen this -- I've already seen his characteristic JB in some documents and this is a little bit -- I don't know. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us about the register where you were shown that the criminal charges and acts from January, February, March were submitted at that time? When did the Velagici crime actually take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime in Velagici occurred on the 28th of September -- the 28th of June, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The end of June or May. And when would this then be expected to be recorded in the register, then, if we're looking at the cases from March?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. How what should be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. I withdraw the question. Tell me, are you aware that proceedings were suspended and that the charges were dropped?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that the charges were dropped or that it was suspended. I received some information later that those guys who committed the deed in Velagici were interviewed at the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka and that they were released to go to the war unit. There were such requests like that and that the actual court proceedings would continue when conditions for that were created, because all the required statements were actually collected or taken by the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Jurisic, the Muslims who remained in Kljuc, did they feel safe enough to come to the police and to report any crimes that they were victims of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I could see, I mostly saw people who lived in Kljuc and its environs, and most of them remained in the areas around Kljuc. There was some five or six suburban areas that belonged to Kljuc, and those people felt more comfortable and more at ease. I remember that they reported even minor details, robberies, attempts, and -- until I saw this in these proceedings here, I was surprised because I thought that that area was very well -- very nicely preserved from destruction and killing and anything else like that. And I think that people were in contact every day in merchants' shops, then they would come back, I would see them at the market on Saturday, and the organs that were functioning were coming to work normally. Particularly where I was, I think the doors were open to all the citizens of Kljuc, just like that -- it was before the war. There were people in Kljuc who were -- who stayed behind, particularly prominent people who were there throughout the war. They socialised with their mates who were there, their colleagues from work, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say more prominent people, who do you mean? Of which ethnicity were these people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant to say was more prominent people as we are prone to say today, these were people whom I knew from political life, public life before the war. There were quite a few of them. And as opposed to some others who might have a different opinion on that, regardless of how much somebody would agree with me or disagree with me, these more prominent people in Kljuc were very tolerant, very conciliatory, and they did everything to overcome all the things that were not all right because they knew the horrors of war. And I met these war -- these people throughout the war, during the time that I was there. I could even name these people if necessary. I could mention the names of people who stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us of which ethnicity these people were? This is what I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking exclusively of members of the Muslim ethnic group. There were some Croats as well, but they were not so many of them because before the war, Kljuc had under 1 per cent of such citizens. As for the Muslims, there was just a difference of 1 per cent or something like that there, so that a large number of people stayed in Kljuc. They even remained after we actually all moved out in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These villages near the town, the Muslim villages that were preserved, were there any paramilitary units there and was there any fighting there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice any fighting in those villages. Perhaps some individuals went somewhere towards Pudin Han or somewhere else, but there was no attack on the town, no problems at all. These houses were all mixed together, Muslim and Serb houses. There were no incidents, and ultimately I think that people protected one another, as was right, and prevented from any major damage being inflicted on anyone. And even today when I pass through Kljuc, I see that those houses are practically untouched as if there had been no war. You could notice some things in odd places, but practically it was all untouched.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness 1D2720. 1D27020.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have a translation, so I would kindly ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what this is briefly and who is reporting whom to the police. 27020. This is the 30th of December, 1992. Are you able to tell us who is the person who is submitting the complaint and can you read the typewritten part where it says what the complaint actually is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's collapse this document. As Defence objected to the admitting of log-book of Prosecutor's document and then put something -- another criminal report to the witness. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Exactly why I stood on my feet, Your Honours, and on top of that incredibly leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could you put your question, Mr. Karadzic, to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 24, line 5, I asked whether Muslims were free to report to the police any crimes committed against them. And the answer starts on line 8 onwards. And I just wanted to show some documents as examples of the things that were reported to the police by the Muslim citizens. Even Serbs reported Serbs, but I don't know if I'm going to show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before putting the question or putting the document, why don't you ask the witness whether he remembers these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I don't know whether he can know each individual person. These people came to the public security station, not to him, but he knows about this occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have another proper opportunity to tender those documents through proper witnesses. I don't think that this witness is capable of commenting on this document. Spend your time more efficiently. It's up to you how to use your time, but as I expressed our concerns, please bear that in mind. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then that witness would have to be me because there is no other witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, the Prosecution stated that Serb crimes against Muslims were ignored. Do you stand by your assertion that this is not correct and that such crimes were also investigated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the assertion that crimes were investigated and reported. However, in the municipality we were not satisfied with all that was done. We felt that more could have been done because later, regardless of the war and the way this was manifested, any attack on property or house especially in places bordering on Kljuc could have been reported. The police was out in those villages and hamlets and houses very frequently, looking into it. I remember that there were criminal reports, minor theft, embezzlement in Kljuc. I would like to emphasise that there were no excesses in Kljuc, no actions of that kind. There were very few killings, nobody was detained. So I think it was an example in the whole region in comparison to other towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation in the municipality? Did you have enough fighters and other things and where exactly where your fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters didn't hear the last sentence of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were the fighters of the Kljuc municipality? Was there enough manpower in Kljuc sufficient to provide security for all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were engaged on three fairly large fronts. Our forces were drawn out. There was the Kupres front, where we gave a battalion to the 7th Kupres Brigade in August 1992. The complete brigade of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade went to the Jajce front. The engineering regiment that we also had to man was engaged at Laniste, it went from unit to unit where it was supposed to carry out its tasks. However, because of a shortage of men at the lines, a lot of civilian police officers were engaged in these war units, combat units, so that there wasn't always a sufficient number of policemen that could efficiently keep everything under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 18431, please. 18431. I'm probably going to tender these criminal reports from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this, please. This is the 22nd of August, 1992, it's already the War Presidency, and it says that the combat operations around Kljuc -- actually, due to the war operations linked to the Jajce municipality, the security situation in the area of Kljuc municipality has been significantly worsened. And then in the next paragraph it says: "A large number of people from the area of Kljuc municipality have been engaged in the war units, so the area of the municipality has been literally unprotected from all sorts of incidents that could arise at any given moment. We are absolutely unable to provide for protection to any prisoner of war," and so on and so forth. So how did this situation reflect as far as you were concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please read slow. Yes, please answer the question. No, I told Mr. Karadzic to read slow when he reads from the document. Now can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did this, what was read in this paragraph, correspond to what you knew about the security situation and the security forces that was supposed to provide security?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the bulk of the police and military forces were engaged in surrounding fronts, and if this is the estimate of the military police and the army that this was insufficient, then I am really not up to agreeing or disagreeing. I know that they were absent, a large number of people. But as for whether this number was sufficient to keep everything under control, that is up to the authorised organs to make that determination. But I think that the forces were stretched thin at the fronts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll accept it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4365, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, yesterday you were asked not to say reproachfully why you did this and that in the area of defence. Can you tell us what sort of powers the municipality had when it came to defence and what did you do, if you did anything, that went beyond the remits of the law?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the developments in Bosnia and the petition that happened, everybody had to do what the majority of the population in a given area asked them to do, where you had an area with a Serb majority or a Muslim majority, you had to keep that in mind. So whatever you did, you were in trouble. One side would insist on you enforcing the law and the other on you not doing exactly that. It was such a situation that no matter who was involved, whether they were president of the republic, whether they were senior officials, everybody felt that they could do things that were above and beyond the law. In the process of mobilisation and the duties incumbent on the Secretariat for National Defence, difficulties began to arise in the month of January when Republika Srpska was proclaimed and when in March the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared. These difficulties came to a head in the month of June, and when it came to mobilising the Territorial Defence we had summoned the entire detachment and the response was good. However, nothing could be done further because the detachment split along the ethnic lines and was dysfunctional. We had the impression that people were somehow advised not to respond to our call-ups. Mr. Asim Egrlic, an SDA official who was also president of the Executive Board, when he was testifying in Sarajevo on one occasion, he confessed that, in September of 1991, they received a message from the head office of the SDA in Sarajevo not to respond to the call-ups. So we were in a paradoxical situation. If the Secretariat for National Defence was the structure that was supposed to have at its disposal all the conscripts, we were in such a situation where the Muslims, in fact, engaged in the recruitment process for the TO and the reserve force of the police but without responding to our call-ups. All of this led us into great difficulties for both sides. We were walking along a very thin line between two sides or else we could side by one of the sides. We had the legislation in force, the JNA wasn't our armed force, and for as long as it was there we respected it. When the VRS was set up, we sided with that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Did you know what the official insignia was in December of 1992 of our forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The army and the police.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was your answer, Mr. Jurisic? Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was I aware of the insignia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was aware of the insignia because I studied international laws of war, which said that in order for a soldier to have that status, he has to wear a uniform with clearly displayed insignia, he has to carry weapons, and he has to have a military commander above him, that's the army. Otherwise, it's not an army, it's just various groups. The insignia is there to show his membership, the weapons to -- for him to fight with, and the commander for him to know what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you touch upon this issue, insignia?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does this arise from the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am about to show the witness, because the witness said that this was something that wasn't done by the regular forces, I was about to ask him what the insignia mentioned in the report refers to. I cannot lead the witness, so I have to lay a foundation and the foundation is in the cross-examination where it was put to the witness that it was done by the regular forces, whereas the witness said that the regular forces were there to protect all the citizens alike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you how to spend your time again. But if the witness said it was done by the regular forces, is it not sufficient? We'll take a break for half an hour. We'll continue at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the witness be shown 1D27020 -- 022.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately we don't have a translation yet because I didn't know these things would be contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'll ask you to delve into this document. On the 8th of December, 1992, the public security station attended a scene where a robbery was committed against Ifeta Sadikovic, Fadil's wife, from Krasulje. What is Ifeta's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you're concerned, can you tell us how did it happen that those from Hripavci and Krasulje came to be temporarily residing in Kljuc? Can you tell us in the capacity that you had as the head of the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure where you're heading. Let's collapse this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies -- [In English] I can tell it in English if you ask witness to remove headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if you could do that. Could you kindly take off your headphones, please, Mr. Jurisic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear us, Mr. Jurisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, but I wasn't hearing the interpretation of what the gentleman was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if you could remove your headphones, please. Yes, Ms. Edgerton first.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just -- I rose because I had no idea what was happening, Your Honours. An untranslated document that was put to the witness in a leading way and I just think when we go too far down this road, we're on the edge of Dr. Karadzic actually manipulating the evidence in re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, first from this document it appears that the police went out on the terrain of the crime scene to investigate a heavy robbery against Muslim citizens. Then it is obvious that the civilians from the -- those villages are moved to the very city under the Serbian control. And finally, in the middle it said that the Muslims described the guys who robbed them and threatened them, so and so, and said that the emblem on their own beret was very big and not usual. And it shows what was alleged by the Prosecution that the people suffered. We see from whom they suffered and what was the position of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you put your question to the witness without putting -- without showing the document? Mr. Jurisic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, what became of the civilians in the villages where there was fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which villages are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, say Krasulje, Hripavci, and in general in the villages where there was fighting going on, what became of the civilians, where were they put up if they did not remain in these villages?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I think they were relocated to safer areas, especially in the village of Krasulje where there was a mopping-up operation. According to a statement in Sarajevo, a great many of them withdraw to a small hill, Galaja, together with others from Sanski Most. So the question was raised of whether they should continue their journey on to Bihac or return to Krasulje. When the mopping-up activities were over, according to what one Muslim stated before the court in Sarajevo, half of them returned to Krasulje. So people would seek refuge temporarily for the duration of the fighting or the mopping-up activities which were taking place, after which they would return home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript says in line 17 that -- it says that you had no idea. Did you say that you had no idea or according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do I have no idea of?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of where the civilians were seeking refuge.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If the victims would describe their perpetrators as having a large emblem on their cap quite untypical, would that have been an emblem of the regular Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not members of the regular Serb forces. Nobody could identify them, either by their uniform or by anything else. Simply put, they were people - I don't know how to put it - the dogs of war who were roaming the area in search of booty and targeting victims. There were attempts to get a grip on them to put them under control of the forces which had a command of their own and had discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If a perpetrator would threaten a victim that nobody should know of what happened or else that person would be killed, what was the intention behind this, then, to conceal this from whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're talking about, conceal from whom. I wasn't involved in that. I suppose there were different cases of blackmail, so those who fell victim to looting would conceal that and be silent on the matter because there were threats made and these threats could be made after misdeeds were perpetrated that fell foul of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the authorities when it came to the destruction of Muslim buildings such as mosques, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the position was to do everything to preserve these buildings. However, there were incidents happening at night, things that were beyond control, but the destruction was inflicted in such a way as to make it quite clear to those who were privy to explosives that these were deeds of amateurs. It was done unprofessionally, so the conclusion could be drawn that these were riotous groups who wanted to clear the terrain for their own ulterior motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 65 ter 893. [In English] There should be a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look on your right-hand side, the 1st of February, 1993, the destruction of a mosque. The Prosecutor requested that an action be taken in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an on-site investigation and the description of the site says that the surroundings buildings were damaged as well as the cellar. Is this what you were talking about, that they would be using large amounts of explosives in an unprofessional way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that when the mosque in Kljuc was destroyed, Serbs have gone through -- had gone through a great deal of fear. During the explosion, pieces of debris were thrown several hundred metres around. The glass panes on the surrounding buildings were smashed. There were people residing in the vicinity. There were some industrial sheds there that were destroyed. The area was populated by both the Serbs and Muslims and they were in fear of their lives because there was great destruction. And as I said, none of the windows on the buildings surrounding the area were left intact. That was the scale of the explosion. I know that an investigation had to be launched against unidentified perpetrators and, to the best of my knowledge, the perpetrators were never identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, did you touch upon this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The destruction of the mosque? No, not at all. And the whole -- this whole last couple of paragraphs of transcript could have been dealt with without showing the witness the document in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does this arise from the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness said was being challenged, namely, that all citizens were protected equally irrespective of religious or ethnic affiliation. What was stated was that there were no criminal reports filed in cases when Muslims were victims. So this is a general challenge to this witness's statement and this is proof that that is wrong. On page 15, for example, there is a challenge regarding the impartiality of the authorities in terms of protection and prosecution of cases where Muslims were the victims. Page 17 speaks of the fear of Muslims, and now we hear that Serbs were afraid too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Excellencies, on page 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in line 20 to 25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said "no," Mr. Karadzic. In terms of general challenge, the Chamber will allow the question. But, Mr. Robinson, I'm forming the impression that Mr. Karadzic is going to use or exhaust 325 hours before he reaches his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, actually we are calculating it and we are leaving 16 hours for his testimony, so he'll have to be disciplined in order to accomplish that, but that's what we're heading for. And if I could also say that I think your ruling that you've just made was correct. But I do think that given the witness's lack of knowledge about the investigative procedures in Kljuc and about what the police did, that it would have been better for Dr. Karadzic to tender these documents through the bar table because I don't think the witness is in a position to add much and it is not a very good use of our time. But anyway, he's free -- and I think what he's doing is legally correct, and so we appreciate that you're willing to allow him to do that and hope that it will still result in him having enough time to give his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And a general question to you, Mr. Jurisic: Are you aware of a single case of a crime committed against a Muslim or a Croat that was hushed up by the authorities or where the authorities rejected the case, did not offer any protection?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that this was not within my line of work but everything that happened that was illegal and unlawful had to be punished. The court of law was supposed to work, the police as well. And I remember once that Mr. Franjo Komarica, the bishop of Banja Luka, directly addressed the president of the Municipal Assembly, Jovo Banjac, asking for the remaining Croats in Kljuc to be protected as well as their Catholic church. In spite of all of these things that were done, later on -- well, the church was of a very light construction and it was easy to torch. So it seems that ultimately some kind of groups of hooligans torched it after all. The authorities never wanted anything like that to happen because this disturbed the Serb and Croat and Muslim population when things like that happened. This is something that people were not used to. It was only the older people who were afraid, but those from the 1950s and 1960s were not familiar with any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, if I may, I would just like to foreshadow that if Dr. Karadzic continues down this route, I'm going to be asking the Court to renew our tender of the log-books that were previously denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, page 86 of yesterday's transcript, it was suggested to you that -- actually, I'm going to read it out exactly and then it's going to be interpreted to you. [In English] "What you said, Mr. Jurisic, was that the action taken up until the 27th of May, 1992, effectively were pursuant to instructions from the top political leaders of the Serbian people; isn't that right? "A. We received all of this that had to do with mobilisation. We received all of that from the command of the military district of Banja Luka." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Today do you stand by that, that you were subordinated to the military district of Banja Luka and that you received orders from them, not from Pale?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just say in two words, that we as the municipal authorities, while the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina functioned, absolutely, we were linked to the republican Secretariat for National Defence, which later after the multi-party elections became part of the Ministry of Defence. So we had this two-way communication. As for all military affairs, we were never directly linked to the secretariat or the ministry; rather, we had a stop in between and that was the command of the military district and it roughly corresponded to the then-area of responsibility of a corps. When the Ministry of Defence was established we remained linked to the command of the military district. So all mobilisation, recruitment, manning of the armed forces, all of these things we received from the military district from Banja Luka. We did not receive anything from Pale at the time, but we could never be directly linked in terms of mobilisation and military matters directly to the highest republic organ. After this reorganisation, we were told that from the 1st of July, 1992, we would belong to the secretariat of the Ministry of Defence that was established at the level of the corps. And then the command of the military district ceased to exist in Banja Luka and two secretariats were formed. The secretariat in Banja Luka that was in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, that was the 5th Corps until then, the 5th Corps of the JNA. However, since the JNA had ceased to exist, well, then our municipality of Kljuc came to belong to the secretariat of the Ministry of Defence in Drvar that covered 12 municipalities in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps, so that was the way things were. We never had these direct links. We had links with the republic organ only as far as regulations were concerned, civilian protection, the service for surveillance, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military part was there -- let me just say one more thing. The Ministry of Defence or previously the Secretariat for National Defence, we never received any instructions directly from them until 1991, when these powers became intertwined. And then from the command of military district we were told that we should send recruits, conscripts to the army. And then from Sarajevo, from the ministry, they send certain telegrams stating that no such persons should be sent and that is when this intertwining took place. When this happened it was for the first time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. What were the links, what was the communication between Kljuc and the centre of the republic, or rather, the government in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the corridor was cut off, it was a generally known thing that all kinds of communication ceased to exist. There were no communications in terms of railways, roads, et cetera. So until the end of June/beginning of July, we did not have any communication until the corridor was reinstated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, two things. I would be able to make my objections in a more timely fashion if Dr. Karadzic and the witness spoke more slowly. And second, there's no way I dealt with anything related to communication in the cross-examination; that's squarely outside of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to express my disagreement. It says here that you received instructions, page 86 yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the communication issue was not raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I'm recollecting it correctly, she did ask questions concerning whether they were following the instructions of the republican authorities, which would go directly to the issue of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And he confirmed. And then -- I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Jurisic, until when did you have a Crisis Staff? When did it grow into the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date, but I think it was the month of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you receive my decision of the 31st of May abolishing the Crisis Staffs? P2608, that's the number for the participants.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that directly. I do not recall that date, whether it was then or some other time. There were so many dates, so many things happened. Without looking at documents, it's very hard for a person to be able to say anything. It was the president of the Crisis Staff, the president of the Municipal Assembly that knew that the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also what was shown here was that you attended certain meetings and you didn't know exactly what these meetings were. Tell me, if there were a rally of citizens from a local commune, if they wanted to be informed about certain preparations, who would they invite from the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the very nature of things, I think they'd invite somebody from the military, the Ministry of Defence, the police. These were the people who were in charge of that structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if the military was not there, who would they ask out of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the president of the Assembly, the president of the Executive Board, the commander of the police, the public security station. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was secretary of the Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to ask you once again, did you receive after the war broke out any instructions from Pale in relation to anything?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as defence was concerned, we did not. The first time I had direct communication regarding defence was with Drvar, August 1992. I came across General Subotic. He was minister of defence and I saw him there and I saw Minister Sajic who was minister of national defence in the AR Krajina over there, when they gave us the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army and when they told us that our organisation that we had had until then, the command of the military district in Banja Luka, that then -- from then onwards it would be the Secretariat for National Defence and that we in the municipality had no further functions, that we could not be in any structures, so that we could fully devote ourselves to defence matters because in some municipalities there were certain challenges. The municipal authorities did not accept what the army and the Ministry of Defence were asking for, so they tried to have as much independence as possible so the people could decide on the basis of regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us in the briefest possible terms during your testimony -- actually, did you have the same position when you testified then as you have today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always have the same position and the same opinion. I did what I did and I always stand by that at any level, at any trial, before any court. I cannot say anything that I do not know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness and Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters did not hear the end of the witness's answer. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said: "I cannot say anything that I do not know."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
