utterances.text: At each trial before each court, during each questioning or when I provide a statement, I say only what I know, what I saw, and about which I'm 100 per cent certain. If something happens like a different word that I would use, perhaps a different word, that is not any change in my position. But simply, a person as a human being is not a tape recorder to be able to be repeat word for word what he said at an earlier occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness 65 ter 26008. English page 3, Serbian 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will read it here. It's there in the Serbian and in the English. You say this: "I think that on the 14th of May, the then Assembly" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you tell the interpreters where you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the main answer of the witness in the Serbian at the bottom of the page. In the English it's: "I am talking about the Assembly session ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here: "I am thinking about the Assembly session in Banja Luka. Since that communication was already difficult at that time, when we received that in writing ..." and so on and so forth. Does that correspond to what you -- today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered about that at the trial of Odanovic Marko before the BH court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was his witness, and when I was saying that, I just had one dilemma and you can see that here in this document, that I said that this was on the 12th or on the 14th of January -- May. However, after I checked and I determined that it was exactly on the 12th of May when a decision of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic -- as a result of which the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Army of Republika Srpska was formed then. And the Territorial Defence did not exist from that time on formally but was transformed into the Army of the Serbian Republic, so that our detachment, which at that time was mobilised, it was no longer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it was part of the 30th Division which was headquartered in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. Witness, we are not able to follow you. Could you repeat when from the -- where you said: Army of the Serbian Republic formed from something, yes. So: "... Territorial Defence did not exist from that time on formally but was transformed into the Army of the Serbian Republic ..." Could you repeat from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. On the 12th of May, 1992, by a decision of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic, the Territorial Defence ceased to exist because a decision was reached that the Yugoslav People's Army should withdraw from the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And since with the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army the Territorial Defence was formed and the detachment of the Territorial Defence in Kljuc which was mobilised at that time became part of the army and became one of the battalions. I don't know exactly the number of the battalion, but it became part of the 30th Division which had its seat in a small barracks, Kula near Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 23. Unfortunately, this page has not been translated, but I'm only going to read two lines. This is the Serbian page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you -- actually, I'm going to read your answer: "Well, I think he was -- all of that perhaps went through at a time when communication was really the most difficult that it ever had been." Do you still stand by this statement of yours that this was the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- when the communications were proceeding with the most difficulty ever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I told you to move on from the topic -- issue of communication. You are not listening to the Chamber's instruction. Move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 20 today you were asked in reference to P3462 about that text by Mr. Banjac, whose signature I asked you about. Are you able to tell us what the rights of the municipality were -- or actually, the defence ministry in relation to the disposal of movable and immovable property during the war and does that disposition mean actually taking over property rights?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking over or assuming property rights, according to the Law on All People's Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that's a leading question. I think the answer's been suggested to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, can you assist us on this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Baird. I think the last -- after "and" made it suggestive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he could ask the question without that part, it would be proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, did the municipality have any rights or the defence have any rights to dispose with property during war time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality and the Secretariat for the National Defence according by law has the right to dispose with all human and material resources which can contribute to the defence of the country. Such facilities, properties, articles are never confiscated on a permanent basis, but are only confiscated for the needs of the army. If the person from whom the property was confiscated keeps the documents indicating that he handed over such property, proceedings are conducted after the war or after the action is completed when the state is obliged to restore the property. And if it is destroyed, it should pay compensation; otherwise, it should return the property if it is unharmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, and I would like to tender page 3 from this document, English page 3, Serbian page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with your leave, Your Honours, I would like to put one document to the witness on the question that Dr. Karadzic asked him, of whether a single case -- whether he was aware of a single case of crime against a non-Serb that was hushed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, you just heard what I asked the Judges of this Chamber, and I'll remind you of Dr. Karadzic's question again. At page 40 of today's temporary transcript, he asked you: "Are you aware of a single case of a crime committed against a Muslim or Croat that was hushed up by the authorities or whether the authorities rejected the case and didn't offer any protection?" And you gave a lengthy answer that was effectively: They never hushed things up. That's what you were saying, isn't it? And if you don't remember your answer, I can read it to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need for you to read my answer back to me. All I would like to ask you is to tell me or to re-phrase that term "hush up." How do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I am asking you the same question Dr. Karadzic gave you in the words he used. The meaning was clear to you obviously in your mind when you gave him a lengthy answer. Your evidence is: There was never any crime committed against Muslims or Croats that were hushed up by the authorities or where the authorities rejected the case and didn't offer any protection. That was your evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer this differently now, but much more specifically. I said that everything that was known, that was reported, the authorities did not ignore that. However, when I was shown everything that was going on, that was the first time that I found out what was going on. I don't know if the authorities knew about it or not. It's difficult to know everything that goes on in the municipality. I did state categorically that the authorities did respond to all of that, but perhaps they did not. When it was presented to me in Sarajevo exactly what was going on, I behaved as if I didn't even live in Kljuc and didn't know what was going on. It was difficult to know what was going on. As for those things that were going on, it's very difficult to establish whether there was any action on the basis of that or not. I doubt that there was enough time to deal with everything and to process everything. There were many things happening all around.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that we did not interpret the sentence before this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, the interpreters missed what you said after you said: "I doubt that there was enough time to deal with everything and to process everything." They think you said something after that that they didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was not possible to have an overview of all that was going on and to register everything because there were some cases that were uncovered much later, when there were no longer any traces left. For example, you find a man who had been killed and that particular incident was not processed. I think that I wouldn't say that that was done intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your answer is you don't know whether any crimes were hushed up, do you? You actually don't know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JURISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I just clarify this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jurisic, could you take off your headphones again kindly. Mr. Karadzic, could you let us know what your question is in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, this question and the answer is so ambiguous in our language, so if the Chamber will take into consideration only "I don't know, I don't know," without what witness said previously, then I have to clarify what he didn't know. But if you take everything into consideration, it's different because of negation in our language: Did you know that something was not -- was or was not hushed up? Or did you know that something was hushed up? This is linguistic catch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In our view, the answer is sufficiently clear. We'll not allow you to put that question. Yes, Mr. Jurisic. Mr. Jurisic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just for the record, Excellencies, I really feel that it is not sufficient to leave that kind of ambiguous questions. So it should be -- he should be asked whether you knew case that was hushed up. Or -- this is difference in language and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: What the witness actually said was that he didn't know whether any case was hushed up or not. It doesn't seem to be very ambiguous. He was saying it wasn't within his sphere of knowledge whether a case was hushed or whether it wasn't. So how one would delve further into that seems very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informed informally from the Registrar that the next witness strongly wishes to conclude his evidence today, which seems almost impossible, unfortunately. While we are waiting, for the record, I wanted to make it on the record that the Chamber issued a confidential decision yesterday vacating its decision to subpoena Mr. Miletic and the subpoena itself. And the Chamber is going to file -- issue a public version of the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just related to the gentleman who's just walked into court, I just wanted to let everyone know that because of the sudden change in the witness schedule the -- and this witness being my responsibility, I haven't yet had an opportunity to correspond whatever exhibits I might want to show in English with the B/C/S original pages. And I'll, of course, over the course of our lunch break try and work to do that as fast as I can, but I might be asking for your leave as well, Your Honours, depending on how the schedule goes for a few extra minutes. I think once I can do that, it would just speed up everything else that happens in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Defence is ready to extend the time if it is possible. I am ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarac. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Sarac, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, and even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might have -- that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Sarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I also understand that you are -- you have been waiting from 9.00 this morning and you wish -- prefer to conclude your testimony today, but given the time I'm not sure it can be done or not due to the scheduling plan of the courtroom. But we'll see how it evolves at the end and then discuss at the end of the day. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sarac.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us please pause between questions and answers. You've already shown that you can do that. Have you provided my Defence team with a statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D8851.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see on the screen before you the first page of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please don't be confused by certain reductions. The Prosecutor asked for certain sentences to be redacted and the Trial Chamber allowed that, and we believe that this does not infringe upon the statement in any way. Did you read and sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the last page so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my signature, the one that I've been using for many, many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this statement faithfully reflect what you communicated to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, but there are two technical errors in two paragraphs, and I would like to ask that that be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us with that, which paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Paragraph 55, the second subparagraph. In paragraph 41 it says -- it should say in paragraph 40 and 41, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. In paragraph 55 you are recalling two paragraphs, 40 and 41?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I think that the same goes for another paragraph, yes, in paragraph 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in paragraph 56, again you are referring to paragraphs 40 and 41?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that be all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as the statement is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: They would be almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement into evidence according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there are three associated exhibits being offered. The first one was omitted from our Rule 65 ter list due to an oversight. We would ask that it be added. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit them all. Shall we assign the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the 92 ter statement 1D8851 will be D4368. 65 ter number 1D00848 will be D4369. 17333 will be Exhibit D4370, and 65 ter number 17446 will be Exhibit D4371.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out a brief summary of Mr. Jovan Sarac's statement in the English language. [In English] Jovan Sarac was born on 19th of February, 1967, in Praca, Pale municipality. He was a member of the SDS Main Board from the -- from July 1991 and a member of the SDS Municipal Board in Pale. In early 1990 the SDA was formed. This made the Serbian people very concerned. Although the Serbs were reluctant to organise politically along ethnic lines, they did so out of necessity in response to the Muslim and Croat action. Upon Dr. Karadzic's election as president of the party at its founding Assembly, Mr. Sarac -- he -- Karadzic did not have much political authority and considered his political engagement to be temporary. The key goals of the party were the preservation of Yugoslavia and the equality of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The party leadership advocated that all political issues in BH be resolved through negotiations. In May 1991, the Muslims formed a paramilitary unit called the Patriotic League. They moved freely Sarajevo, half-uniformed, and with the emblems of that paramilitary organisation. The law enforcement did nothing although they were illegal. The Serbs at that time had no paramilitary organisations. With regards to the arming of the Muslims, the JNA discovered the theft of the weapons and the mines and explosives from the JNA barracks in Renovica municipality of Pale, carried out by some Muslims. After their arrest, there were mass protests among the Muslims in Bistrik, Sarajevo, demonstrating a lot of hatred and primitivism surrounding the command of 2nd Army district. The aim of the theft was to arm the Muslim paramilitary formations. The murder of the Serbian wedding guest in Bascarsija was followed by a number of incidents. Cars and buses were intercepted on the Sarajevo-Pale road and money and documents were seized from the passengers. It was done by the Green Berets. On April the 4th, 1992, Muslim extremists beat up two bus drivers and some Serbian passengers. The Green Beret attacks are purely -- attacked a purely Serbian village, Lapisnica, and wounded one person. After this, the police from Pale intervened and protected the local Serbian population. Then a check-point was set up in Lapisnica between Pale and Sarajevo. Both the JNA military police and the regular police were in charge of it. With regard to the moving of the Muslims, the Serbian authorities in Pale considered that all the citizens should stay and their rights, safety, and property should be guaranteed. Nevertheless, many Muslims asked to be allowed to leave Pale. The local authorities tried to convince them this was not necessary, and the Crisis Staff assured that they would provide full protection for all its citizens regardless of their religion and ethnic situation. The SJB had the authority to grant the requests of moving. If the Muslims wished to leave, police escorts would be provided. Later most Muslims were escorted in convoys, secured by the local police, to the line of separation in the surrounding of Sarajevo without any incident. In July 1992, after a meeting, the Executive Committee of the Pale Municipal Assembly issued a conclusion on the obligation of the police station to protect the property of Muslims. After the conflict, all Muslim property was returned to its owners. The Croats from Pale did not ask to move and they stayed in Pale during the conflict and after it. And that is the summary. At that moment I don't have questions for Mr. Sarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you prefer to have a lunch break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would, Your Honours, and I'll work at speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sarac, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement instead of your oral testimony. And after the lunch break you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall have a break of -- for 40 minutes and resume at ten to 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sarac.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to start by asking you just a couple of questions about the statement you gave to Dr. Karadzic's Defence that he showed you here a few minutes ago. Could you just explain how did it work? Did you get this as a draft or did you write the whole thing yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I gave the statement to the investigators -- to an investigator, Mr. Furtula, and it was partly supplemented during my conversation with President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when you gave that statement, did you have documents with you? Did you use documents?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Of course. I used all the documents that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were they your own documents or were they shown to you by the investigator or was it a mix of both?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: It was a mix of both.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in your statement where you quote some things, like at paragraph 5 where you quote a speech from Dr. Karadzic, you found that quote in a document; it's not something you remembered?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you -- you wrote in some detail about minutes of Main Board meetings. Did you do that from your memory or do you have a notebook?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I did that on the basis of my own notes that I kept while I was a member of the Main Board. I did that at the sessions that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when -- in that collection of documents that you had and the Defence gave you initially, did you review any military documents, either from the JNA or the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Well, I reviewed military documents that I considered to be relevant for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what military documents were those?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: It was, first of all, the Law on Defence and Protection of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; and then the Law on Defence and Protection of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and then different bylaws that pertained to defence, the Law on Armed Forces of the SFRY, the Law on Defence of Republika Srpska, the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, an order on the application of rules of international law in Republika Srpska, instructions on how to act with prisoners of war, and other documents that I may remember as we continue to talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that collection of documents you reviewed, did you see any documents with evidence, for example, that Bosnian Serb forces sought territory in which Muslims were a majority?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: For the most part I read regulations, but absolutely nowhere did I find a document instructing the armed forces of Republika Srpska to take territories where the Muslims constitute the majority population. However, I'm saying that I read regulations for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And now when you met Dr. Karadzic or his Defence team here on the day that you signed this statement, did you review more documents?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: In the meantime, most of these documents that I found to be important, I took them along and I re-read them by way of preparation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the rest of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear what you said after "re-read them by way of preparation." Would you be able to repeat?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Most of the documents on the basis of which I gave this statement, I took along and I read them, not the entire documents, but those parts that I considered to be relevant. I did not have any additional documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So in your proofing with Dr. Karadzic here, you were not shown any additional documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: A moment ago I received just one document from the President that has to do with the minutes of the session of the Executive Board of the SDS. I got that just as I was walking into this room. I think that the document is not particularly relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now just about your jobs, am I correct if I say that you became president of the Pale SDS Municipal Board in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And am I also correct if I say that you were a member of the Crisis Staff for Pale in April, May, June, and July 1991 -- 1992, pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, ex officio, I was a member of the Crisis Staff in the period of -- well, the Crisis Staff functioned in Pale only for about two months.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what function did you serve then after that period of time where the Crisis Staff, as you said, ceased functioning?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: You mean professionally where I was?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, actually, there's not -- when you talked in your statement about the functions you served, there's actually not a single date reference as to the terms of office that you held except when you added something to your statement here to say you served with the Main Board until 1996. So what were you doing in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I started working in the Ministry of the Interior and I was a desk officer for legal affairs. After that, in roughly 1994, again, I was a counsellor for legal affairs in the Ministry of Defence. Throughout this time I was a member of the Main Board of the SDS and president of the Municipal Board of the SDS in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, just before I move on to another area, when you talked about the document that you received from Dr. Karadzic, when exactly did you receive it? Just a few minutes ago or before you came into this courtroom and took the oath to testify?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I received it when I came here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, was that just a few minutes ago, while we were on the lunch break?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No, no, when I came here, when I came here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Now, just in terms of your work with the Crisis Staff, is it also -- can you also confirm that for a period of time you were on the Crisis Staff for SAO Romanija?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No, the -- there never was a Crisis Staff for Romanija, never existed. There was an Assembly of SAO Romanija and there was a government of SAO Romanija and there was a regional board for the SDS for Romanija. A Crisis Staff never existed at regional level as far as the SAO Romanija is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at 65 ter number 21353, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this is from -- it's a newspaper article, you can see, from "Oslobodjenje" dated 26 March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Sarac would be helped if you actually made the one in his language bigger.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Although you can understand and read English, I think, can't you, Mr. Sarac?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you enlarge the one in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this newspaper report says that -- it's still really, really tiny, but if you can go down to, I think, the third full paragraph, it says that Malko Koroman asserted he had terminated the five non-Serb police officers in Pale and three in Sokolac on the order of the government of SAO Romanija. So who gave him the order then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Well, Malko Koroman was chief of the public security station in Pale. He could have possibly issued an order like that for Pale, but not for Sokolac because Zoran Cvijetic was the chief of the public security station there. So I mean -- I don't know if that's the way it was, who it was that could have issued that order to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was in the government of SAO Romanija that would have issued the order to Malko Koroman? That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: The minister of the interior was Zoran Cvijetic. He was minister of the interior of the SAO Romanija. As I've already said, SAO Romanija did not have a Crisis Staff but a government that functioned up until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not sure about the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you were a member of the Assembly of SAO Romanija; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No, I was just a member of the regional board of the SDS for Romanija.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe when this is listened to they're going to correct this, but line 8, the witness said that it was until October 1992 that the government functioned, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Sarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that this has to be checked. I think that all governments were abolished then but I'm not sure. It's not that it worked with particular intensity. Perhaps it was earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking your answer -- what your answer was because the interpreters missed it. What did you say, up until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that the government worked until October 1992, but that is just on the basis of memory. I don't have a single document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you talked -- we'll move on to 1992. And you spoke at paragraph 22 about a declaration of imminent threat of war and mobilisation of the Territorial Defence on the 15th of April. Now, you know, don't you, that that decision of the 15th of April was actually militarily implemented the following day, on the 16th? It's not a trick question. Would you agree with me that the decision was militarily implemented the next day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, mobilisation cannot be implemented as fast as that. It's a lasting process.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at another document, maybe I'll be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: P2412, please. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is the decision to -- to the government of the autonomous regions and the Serbian autonomous regions, to all the Serbian Assemblies on the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go over to page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see the decision was issued by General Subotic, who was a minister at the time. And paragraph 2 of this document -- or, pardon me, paragraph 1 says: "The municipal Territorial Defence staffs that have operated regularly so far shall remain in the same formation and establishment ..." And that's actually what was happening in Pale, wasn't it, their mobilisation had been effected and the Territorial Defence in Pale was functioning; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The command of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Pale was functional practically until the VRS was set up with some small exceptions, because it had been operational from the earlier period, the entire structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From the earlier period actually predating this order; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then let's look at another document. Maybe you can confirm it for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P6094. This is a 2nd Military District Command document and it's dated April 8th, 1992. And if we can go over to the second page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under the heading "4th Corps" --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And let me just see if I have the right page in B/C/S because I don't have paragraph numbers. I think you have to go back to the first page in B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under the heading "4th Corps," second paragraph, it says: "During the afternoon, the members of the Territorial Defence from Pale municipality opened mortar fire on the sector Vratnik and on the old part of the city of Sarajevo ..." So not only was the Territorial Defence in Pale functioning at that point in time even before the forces were implemented, it was shelling parts of the old town of Sarajevo. That's what this contemporaneous document shows; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: It's a document of the JNA which I have no knowledge of. I can tell you that, under the law, the TO units were resubordinated to the JNA. Until the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina that was the case. There could have been a paramilitary organisation, a volunteer group, or somebody doing things wilfully, but I'm not privy to the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this document - if you go over to the second page - it's a standard military daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Second page in B/C/S, please. And then again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The signatory - and you can go over to the last page as well - the signatory, Slobodan Tripkovic, member of rank, is doing this job. The man who signed this document, the duty team, has an obligation, Mr. Sarac, to make sure his information is accurate because he's sending it up to his command. It doesn't say anything about any kind of renegade here, any kind of wilful behaviour, does it? Are you saying he got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I simply don't have any information about the contents of this document. I'm not an expert that could comment on who could take decisions or issue orders, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Fine. We'll move on. I want to go to that part of your statement where you talk the 400 men from Bratunac and it's at paragraph 41. Now, in the first draft of your statement, Mr. Sarac, you said that: "The local or republican leadership never found out how these people had been captured or why they were transferred to Pale ..." And then in what you finally signed, you amended that evidence to read: "The local leadership never found out why these people were transferred to Pale, whereas the republican leadership was out of town in Banja Luka at an Assembly session ..." So you changed your evidence, right, because it appears from what you now say, you knew how these people had been captured?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: We never came to learn how these people were captured. This amendment to my statement was due to the fact that subsequently I found out that the entire republican leadership was out of town attending an Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you even see these 400 men come into Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in a cafe at a time when these trailer-trucks carrying these people came to Pale. We tried to notify the republican leadership at once; nobody knew anything. They spent four days at Pale. We were trying to help them through the Red Cross by providing them with food, blankets, and so on. They were put up in the gym because they had to be put somewhere. We tried to find out where they had come out and learnt that some paramilitaries who wore the red berets did that, that the goal behind their actions was to discredit Pale and the republican leadership. After having spoken to President Karadzic and President Krajisnik and -- or rather, President Krajisnik and President Djeric, because President Karadzic was away, we insisted that these people be released, and the fact is that they were all in civilian uniforms. We had full support. Later on President Karadzic came, appropriate orders were issued, and these people were transferred to Muslim-controlled territories. I think that they only spent four days at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would have seen, then, that these men were physically abused, like they had been bruised and they had been beaten and they been mutilated, you would have seen that; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: There were no visible injuries. I don't know if there were injuries that could be observed. I didn't spend a great deal of time there. Right away with the deputy and president of the Crisis Staff, I busied myself with trying to find out what can be done with these people and how they can be assisted, and in fact this was seen through to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you spoke about Renovica as well in your written evidence. It was the Crisis Staff's decision to send the police to Renovica on 22nd of May, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the chief of the police station settled with their leader that they should surrender weapons, and it was the police patrol that was supposed to do that. It was not a decision, it was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said it wasn't a police action but a police patrol and "action" wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Sarac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a police patrol which, based on the agreement between the chief of the police station and the leaders of the Muslims in the area, which was supposed to do this. It came under fire and two policemen were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the person who commanded that operation was Malko Koroman; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The question stated that it was an operation, whereas the witness clearly said that it was a patrol.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I concur fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you know, Mr. Koroman actually some years ago was interviewed by the ICTY and the interview was audio recorded. And he spoke about that operation, and I'd like to have a look at that transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 26014. And we could go, when we get it, to page 76.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's, unfortunately, not available in your language, but are you able to read it, Mr. Sarac, or would you like me to read it to you and have it translated, the portions I'd like to put to you? It's your choice.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: It's best that it's interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. In this main -- this large paragraph that you see on the page in front of you, Mr. Koroman talks about that action and he says: "I participated and I know of that action, it's in regard to a part of Pale ... where some 90 to 92 per cent of the population were Muslims and maybe some 87 per cent were Serbs ..." Although I don't know quite how that mathematically works out. And he said further: "There were army barracks there, storage mostly, a lot of ammunition ..." And that's correct, isn't it, both at Renovica and Donja Vinca, those are the old JNA storage facilities for their logistics brigades; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he says: "In May, then, Muslims prevented police from Pale arriving into Renovica and we received an order to establish order in that part of the municipal territory." And then he goes on to talk about how he went there, he says that they were in police uniforms and one of their "targets was to secure the barracks as well because certain groups were entering the barracks and taking ammunition ..." So we'll go over to the next page. I'll tell you what Mr. Koroman said and I'll ask you a couple of questions. And at the next page he says that -- he says they came without a military formation and when they arrived in Renovica they were shot at by the Muslims, two policemen were killed -- although he says some policemen were killed, five or six were wounded. And then he says: "Then 200 inhabitants were not what I would say detained, they were taken into custody, our custody, they were held at the school at Renovica ..." And then they found -- on that occasion they encountered 35 or 37, maybe 33 men who surrendered with weapons and they took them with us to the police station at Pale and he says that they were sent to Kula 10 or 15 days later. And at the very bottom of the page he said: "We handed over the barracks to the army ... and that was the very last day that the police entered Renovica." So my question to you is: You can confirm that there were actually people from Renovica held in the hall behind the police station at Pale as well; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: You see, the police station did have a room where it kept suspects of criminal offences. That was the case before the war, during the war, and today. In this case, it obviously had to do with a police patrol whose objective was to enforce the rule of law in that part of the Pale area, which was within the purview of the Pale SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What size of patrol is required to take in more than 230 people into custody?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I absolutely doubt that that was the number of the persons involved. I don't think that it was possible at all. There could not have been more than 10 to 15 people. Was this an error? There was strange circumstances. People were afraid, people gave different statements, perhaps to accommodate someone. I don't know. I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're saying Mr. Koroman, who you said did everything he could to help the Muslims, and you described him in your statement as a man of integrity, you're saying Mr. Koroman got it wrong when he said this in this audio-recorded interview with the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I'm absolutely certain that no more than 15 individuals were captured in this particular -- on this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is that because you were in your capacity as a member of the Crisis Staff receiving reports on the operation? How else would you know?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes. He informed us of it at the meeting of the Crisis Staff and it had to do with a small number of people. We insisted that these individuals, if they were not guilty, should be released at once; and if guilty, should be transferred to Kula and placed in the jurisdiction of the prosecutor's office. After all, there has to be documentation indicating this and it would have to have been part of the records of the Kula prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the evidence is actually, Mr. Sarac, that the prisoners from Renovica actually weren't released to Kula until the 11th of July. So you're quite right, but the transfer took some time. That's actually the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No. The last -- or actually, after the departure of this group of 400 Muslims from Bratunac, there were no more -- they were transferred to Kula far sooner.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, what I'd like to put to you is, Mr. Sarac, that Mr. Koroman's accounting of the events is actually far closer to reality than your assertions that you're giving us now. The Crisis Staff, I'll put to you, gave the order to Mr. Koroman to assume control over the area. He reported to you about the operation and he calls it an operation, and the evidence before this Chamber is that he came to Renovica with dozens of soldiers. One witness said about a hundred soldiers, which is completely consistent with the size of forces he would need to take effective control over the area. It's actually in your interests, isn't it, to say that the incident was of a much smaller scale than even Mr. Koroman told us?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I'm absolutely certain that the incident was of a much smaller scale, more than ten-fold. I don't know which police forces were involved in this. It is possible that at the time -- I suppose that the SJB had a hundred policemen overall in the station so they could not have spared more than a dozen, but I'm sure that the Defence can call Mr. Koroman and ask him to explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before I move on, could I have these two pages tendered as Prosecution exhibits, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think they've been put -- fully put to the witness and we don't normally admit these statements which are considered for the purpose of litigation. So I don't think that there's any -- it's not part of our practice to admit it, and since it's been put to the witness there's no reason to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see your point. Do we need to admit Mr. Koroman's interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could just have your indulgence, I'll have a word with Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sarac, are you similarly so sure that no one in the gym, the hall behind the police station at Pale was beaten?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I have to information about that. I did not receive information that there had been mistreatments.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you actually said in your statement that it was untrue. Are you now saying that you simply have no information about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: According to the information I had, it is not true that people were mistreated in the gym.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, even Dr. Karadzic's -- one of Dr. Karadzic's Defence witnesses who you know, Mr. Hrsum - pardon me for the mispronunciation - said he couldn't rule it out, and that's at transcript page 32942. He said: Well, I can't say that maybe there were no abuses by those who secured the premises or that maybe they allowed entry to certain individuals. And then Mr. Koroman in this same document - if we could go to page 88 - actually confirms that. At the bottom of this page he said: "I received information, maybe on some second or third day, from a worker of mine, Tomislav," and the last name is misspelled which is Vrsan, "that there are individuals from those units who are entering the gym and harassing the detainees." And he said Mr. Hrsum informed him because he knew that he would stand up for them - you can go over to the next page - for their protection. So police officials, one of whom who gave evidence under oath here and the other one who stated this in an audio-recorded interview, have both said that they couldn't rule out the possibility that there were beatings. And this Chamber has heard that prisoners in the gym were called out by name by soldiers they knew and beaten, one man until he passed out, and the beating only stopped when a soldier came up and told them they were beating the wrong guy. That soldier, this witness said, was Milomir Tepis, and that's at transcript page 15304 to 05 and P2839. And Milomir Tepis has actually -- was convicted in 1999 to 13 years' imprisonment for the beatings of prisoners committed at the Dom Kulture in Pale, that hall. So two police officials with control over the institution have said it could be possible, and a court in your own country has actually convicted one of the perpetrators and you don't have that information, as a man who was a member of the Crisis Staff of Pale at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I remark that paragraph 57 speaks about beatings by guards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's totally inappropriate to intervene in such a way. Yes, Mr. Sarac, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I said was that I as a member of the Crisis Staff did not get information that they were mistreated and beaten there. People in the police station who were directly responsible for that probably knew that. Under the Law on Common Affairs that was under their jurisdiction. So I was only talking about the information that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So why didn't you say that in your statement, that you simply didn't know and had limited information at your disposal, rather than saying that it was untrue that prisoner were beaten?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Could you please just help me by telling me which paragraph that is?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can do that in one second, no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I may help, 57, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, paragraph 57. At paragraph 57 you said these facts are not true.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: And then I go on to say, according to what I know, none of the detainees were mistreated, which doesn't mean necessarily that there were no incidents. Which was later something that was confirmed by those.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Well, then I have a question actually. In your statement from paragraph 50 -- in paragraph 51, 52, 54, 55, 56, 57, and so on, 58 and 59, you've said a series of incidents, assertions, claims, aren't true. How, then, are we to take that based on the qualification you've just made in your statement? Does that mean you simply -- when you say it's not true, does that mean you simply just don't know?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I can say what I know about each of these particular cases. You cannot apply the principle in general to each of these situations because each one is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Ms. Edgerton's question is this: When you say all these facts are not true, can we understand it to mean that according to the information you had those facts were not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you talked about paramilitary forces in Pale, saying that there -- initially there were no paramilitary organisations and then there was one unit called Charlie's Unit which was terrorising the population. And then saying at paragraph 53 that the paramilitaries were banned and prosecuted, but that's actually not the case, is it? Even two months after Dr. Karadzic's order banning paramilitaries, Arkan's men were staying at the Hotel Panorama.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: My statement says that these were not Arkan's men, but a unit commanded by a certain Charlie. This unit did not take part in any fighting. It exclusively looted and terrorised the local population, regardless of their ethnicity. We did notice this problem, we informed the top leadership, including President Karadzic and the defence minister and others from the corps command. After that, a unit was engaged from Trebevic and a police unit, and then they expelled that unit from Pale. After that, no paramilitary unit participated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Tell us when that happened.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I assume that that could have been sometime in June 1992, but I'm not absolutely sure. You know, it was a -- it was a difficult thing to do, to expel that unit. It was a trained, well-organised and well-armed unit. A lot of time was required to be able to do that, and our people, military and civilian commanders who were conducting the operation carried out the operation without a single error.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also in your statement you said at paragraph 9 that Karadzic was a leader who had no control over the army and certain parts of the government. But you weren't a soldier during the war, were you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No. I worked at the Ministry of Internal Affairs as a civilian and then I worked at the Ministry of Justice. I was a civilian working on legal affairs in both institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you never attended meetings of the Supreme Command; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: That is correct. As an SDS official, I think that I would not have been allowed to attend anyway. Everybody knew who members of the command were and they attended and then somebody else could be invited to the meeting for very specific reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You wouldn't have seen any of Dr. Karadzic's military directives or any of his orders to the military?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No. I just saw those that were published, that is, the order on the application of international law in the armed forces as well as instructions on the treatment of prisoners of war. I did not have access to others that were issued because probably they were also confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You weren't present at his meetings with his military anywhere in the war theatre; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No. I was at a meeting with him only once when -- this was in 1995 and it was dealing with military issues, and this was in 1995 when the order was issued to re-direct the Trebevic Battalion to a different area and that another unit from the Krajina come to that area. That was when they asked me from the command to use my authority to try to speak with President Karadzic because many saw conspiracy in it. Many of them heard stories that that area was supposed to fall, that it was supposed to be traded off for Gorazde. I spoke with Mr. Karadzic. I said that people were concerned, that there was a number of people who were prepared to leave for fronts in other areas, but we were concerned because that area could fall because nobody would defend that area except the people who lived there. I did encounter a lot of understanding. President Karadzic called General Mladic and he explained to him what the problem was. He did not have an attitude of issuing orders to him in the sense that he was ordering him to do something. He said that he knew about the problem and that he thought that that unit could achieve certain results, but in view of the fact that the citizens were concerned about it, that measure would be reviewed and that was done so that the Trebevic Battalion remained at Trebevic. And thank God the enemy forces did not manage to take Pale in that offensive on the Sarajevo front, precisely thanks to that move.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was in August 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also weren't party to Dr. Karadzic's conversations with any members of his Main Staff, other than this one incident that you've just described to us, you weren't a part of those conversations; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No. I was in President Karadzic's office as he spoke to General Mladic on the phone. I never attended any meeting with the military leadership, it wasn't something that my position would permit me to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that conversation on the phone refers to this single meeting that you've just told us about in August 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes. He called General Mladic in my presence, he explained what the problem was, and he received the promise that the order would be withdrawn, the order about the reassignment of the Trebevic Battalion to a different theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So really what you've told to us, you weren't anywhere in the military chain of command; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Correct, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this Court has actually received a great deal of evidence about how the command and control of the army actually worked from the people who were a part of it. General Gvero, even way back in 1992, explained it to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and I'll tell you what he said. It's from D422, e-court page 63 and B/C/S pages 62 and 63 in English. General Gvero said: "Shortly, the basic elements are there's the Supreme Command of the army, and that's the president as the supreme commander, and in our situation this will be the Presidency. All the elements of defence and the army are subordinated to this institution. We in the army are following this and trying to fully observe it ..." So that is a very clear contemporaneous statement by one of Dr. Karadzic's senior commanders about how the line of command was supposed to function and how it did, they were doing what they were told; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: You have that in the constitution and in the Law on the Army. The president of the republic is the supreme commander, but he's not authorised or responsible in the operational sense. He cannot issue orders specifically to a unit. His authority is set by the republican constitution, the Law on Defence, the Law on the Army. So it's a little bit broader of aspect of command of the armed forces, which include some civilian structures as well. But as for the armed forces, the principle that applies there is the principle of subordination and singleness of command. These principles are important in the Yugoslav People's Army and they're still in force today. I think they apply in all countries of the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to show you an order from Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P4925. All right. This is an order, it's a document that's entitled: Amendment or supplement to directive 6 and it was issued by Dr. Karadzic on the 12th of December, 1993. And we could go to paragraph 2, subsection 2, in both languages, so that's on the same page in English. But on the B/C/S document you'd have to go over to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is an order, Mr. Sarac, that says: By -- I'll wait until we see the document. It says: By 21 December 1993 when the Geneva negotiations are resumed to improve the SRK -- the SRK's operational and tactical position by seizing Zuc and Mojmilo to ensure the most favourable position for dividing the town of Sarajevo. All right. You see that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I can hardly see anything it's so dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think what we need to do is in the B/C/S go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you can't see, you should just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Go to the paragraph at the bottom of the page, please, and enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. These are the tasks that Dr. Karadzic issued to the VRS, very specific military tasks, with a view to improving the position for the division of the city before the Geneva negotiations. And we could probably, if it's all right with Mr. Sarac, go over to page 2 now at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: And if you can just zoom in a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. This tactical order was implemented by General Mladic two days later, on the 14th of December, he issued an order to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and he said in the order on the basis of the decision reached by the highest officials of the Serbian people - and it's P3052 - he issued the order to take over control of Zuc, Orlic, Hum, and Mojmilo, among others, to finally provide conditions for the division of Sarajevo. And then the day after that, on the 14th of December, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps issued a command to carry out the operation. So that's P1196. And I can show you any of these things if you'd like to see them. But what I want to put to you is not only do we have contemporaneous statements of people in the direct chain of command, this Court has military documents illustrating the effectiveness of Dr. Karadzic's tactical as well as strategic control. So your assertion that Dr. Karadzic didn't have control of the army actually has no basis in the facts; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I didn't say that he didn't have control of the army. He had supreme control. All of this is legitimate. This is a directive that was submitted to the Main Staff for implementation. One must differentiate between the supreme commander and the operations commander. He has nothing to do with the actual execution of the assignments, but must just say what the tasks are and what the goals would be that would need to be implemented before each peace conference. This was something that was done by each of the sides. This is something that is being done in Syria now as well. I just want to add, I'm a little bit surprised, I'm being treated as if I were a military expert. I'm asked to look at military documents. I wish that I were, but unfortunately I am not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, your written evidence says at paragraph 9 that Dr. Karadzic was engaged in peace plans and unable to keep things under control, especially when it came to the armed forces. Making an assertion like that, Mr. Sarac, it's for me to inquire what the basis of your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes. I assert that most of the time President Karadzic dealt on preparing ways to resolve the situation and seek peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He did not deal that much with the work of the government even though he did have that right under the constitution to convene the government in the same way as the armed forces. The reason for that was because he was busy with these other things and didn't have enough time. My subjective assessment is that he actually liked that part of the job the best because of his profession of psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it's not that Dr. Karadzic couldn't keep things under control when it came to the army, he just liked to do other things better?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Well, there was a great antagonism between the military and civilian organs. A couple of times President Karadzic tried that but he didn't manage to. In the war, authority and power lies in the hands of those who have the weapons; the prime minister, the president do not. So that is a fact, at least when we're talking about these local wars, that's how it is. In my statement, among other things, as an example it says that we in the municipality as civilian structures were not satisfied with the work of the police station. We pointed to a series of problems. It was agreed with the minister of internal affairs, Mr. Stanisic, to make cadre changes. A thousand people assembled and prevented the implementation of the decision to which there was a right, according to the law. Can you imagine how it was then if a minister could not resolve a question in his own backyard, you can imagine how it was then on a broader level.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarac, could you repeat the last sentence of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the question is how effective the government is of the president, the Chief of the General Staff. I mentioned an example from Pale where they tried to legally replace the head of the police station, but this was prevented by a crowd of rabble collecting. The prime minister and the president did not have that power. I know what their authority was, but simply the minister of defence, of the interior were not able to actually exercise the power that they had the right to under the law. That's the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, even though you might have sensed some antagonism between the military and the civilian organs, you're not saying that there was any cracks in the civilian-military machine, are you? Because Dr. Karadzic himself said at the 50th Assembly Session, P970: "How can there be a split between the supreme commander and his subordinate commander? There's no split. If there's a split, it's clear who will have to go. I haven't resorted to firing Mladic or any of his assistants ..." And he never did, did he? Things continued to function; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: You see, you have to understand statements of this sort as a show that you're putting on for the people. It was necessary to appease the masses. The point behind this statement was to reassure people that there were no conflicts, that everything was fine, so as to avoid having people in general siding with one or the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Things --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript doesn't reflect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 23, before "it was necessary to appease," the witness said that there was a rift, a conflict, but it was necessarily -- necessary to conceal this before the masses, but there was a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said so, Mr. Sarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Ms. Edgerton, for planning purposes, I'd like to know how much longer you would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A good half an hour, certainly no less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So to go back to my question, you're not saying that the RS stopped functioning? You're not saying that the civilian-military leadership of the Republika Srpska broke down, are you? Things kept running.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: As I said, the people involved were clever people so ultimately some sort of a compromise was found. Had this conflict come out into the open, I don't think that we would have Republika Srpska today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also said that Dr. Karadzic had trouble controlling his own government. I wonder, have you been watching this trial at all, Mr. Sarac?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So would you have seen Mr. Djeric, Dr. Karadzic's prime minister, coming to testify in his defence and telling all of us that President Karadzic and Krajisnik were the Alpha and Omega of the government? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Prime Minister Djeric was a Prosecution witness for the information of Ms. Edgerton. And while we're at it, making corrections, Dr. Karadzic did attempt to discharge General Mladic on the 4th of August, 1995, so it would be good to put -- if you're going to put broad questions, to make sure they're accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see that? And, yes, he was a Prosecution witness. I just have a note delivered to me from Mr. Tieger to that effect as well. My mistake. Did you know about Prime Minister Djeric's testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not follow the testimony of the former Prime Minister Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for a reference that by testifying in my case, Djeric said that Karadzic and Krajisnik were the Alpha and the Omega.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Transcript page 27952.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, again in front of the Republika Srpska Assembly, this time in 1993, the 34th Session, which is P1739, Dr. Karadzic himself spoke about his relationship with the government. And at English page 255 and B/C/S page 289 he said: "I usually don't do other things except for representing the republic and watching over the internal politics, but believe me, the government is mine. I am responsible for its functioning. I appoint and propose the government mandator. I have a brilliant relationship with Vlado Lukic," the prime minister at the time, "we're often together, he often comes to my cabinet ..." So, Mr. Sarac, Dr. Karadzic in his own contemporaneous statements and his prime minister in front of these Chambers contradict you; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: You see, this too could only be a show for the public. What I said - and you didn't quote this from my statement - was that he did not even have control over some parts of the government. I attended an Assembly meeting and I recall being surprised by a question that was put by the president, who said that he didn't know what became of the money that was coming from the Central Bank, from the mission. His purview was foreign affairs, culture, defence in part, whereas for the rest there were strong individuals in place who were very hard to exercise control over. Of course, under the constitution, the president appoints the prime minister designate. In exceptional cases he may call a meeting of the government, even chair the meeting. I think that the president availed himself of this possibility only in a handful of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your statement, to go on to another area, at paragraph 20 you were also very clear in the point that the Crisis Staffs in the territory of the Serb republic had no command over the armed forces and, more specifically, the JNA. So --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Of course, this is common knowledge. The Crisis Staffs did not have the power to command the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, the TO units, or the police units. The Crisis Staffs were in fact set up pursuant to the federal Law on All People's Defence and the Law on People's Defence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because conditions were not in place for War Presidencies to be declared pursuant to a declared state of war. The Crisis Staffs did not have any powers to command in the field of defence and protection. As I said earlier, when it came to the armed forces, the principles of subordination and singleness of command apply.
