Had the Crisis Staffs had any sort of power over the military and the police, it would in actual fact have meant that there was two-track command in place which is not something that existed under the SFRY military doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're not disputing that the Crisis Staffs were the highest authority in the municipalities, are you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs had the sort of powers that the Municipal Assembly would have in peace time. So the Crisis Staffs were duty-bound to hand-over all the decisions they had taken to the Municipal Assembly for confirmation at the earliest opportunity. This is what were earlier -- in the earlier period the committees for emergency situations or councils for national defence that existed in all municipalities. So this was some sort of an extended Executive Board because one would automatically become a member of these committees for national defence, although you had the possibility of co-opting additional members. I can even cite the articles of the relevant legislation pursuant to which Crisis Staffs were set up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 24 the witness said this was a transformation of what were earlier these committees for emergency situations. So this was a transformation of these structures into Crisis Staffs, and this isn't in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Sarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're giving us a very formalistic approach. You haven't actually looked at any Crisis Staff documentation from anywhere across the breadth of the RS, perhaps outside of your own municipality, Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I reviewed all the documents of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Pale, and I can claim with absolute certainty that all the decisions were taken in accordance with the legislation in force at the time. I was not reviewing the decisions issued by other Crisis Staffs, but of course I always take a legalistic approach. I'm a lawyer by profession. I always follow the same line of thinking, and that's my view today, the one that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so I take it you weren't, in March of 1992, at the RS Assembly on the 27th, P1634, when Dr. Karadzic said, at English page 23, B/C/S page 39, when he said to the delegates: When you return to your municipalities, especially the newly formed ones, establish Crisis Staffs and find a number of reserve officers for those staffs and have them register everyone who owns weapons as well as units. And when he said: They should organise Territorial Defence, and if the JNA is there, they must be placed under command. So this is Dr. Karadzic specifically instructing not only the formation of Crisis Staffs, but what forces should be placed under their command. You weren't there to hear that, were you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: No. But if it's a transcript, I have no reason to doubt the contents and I don't see anything untoward in them. In the former Yugoslavia and later on in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, there was the so-called concept of All People's Defence and social self protection. All the socio-political communities from the local community to the municipality to the republic to the federation had to have plans for emergency situations, combat scenarios, et cetera. The political organisations had to have them as well, such as the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarac --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Later on when the --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarac --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- you actually answered my question in one syllable when you began speaking. And if you want to not stay here so long, perhaps we could try and abbreviate this. And if you want to tell Dr. Karadzic any of these things in his re-direct examination, you could feel free. I want to go on to one last area and it's about the non-Serbs in Pale. Is your evidence that all the citizens of Pale were treated equally and that there were no distinctions made between Serbs and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: From -- on the part of the municipal authorities, but not between the municipal and republican --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you think you could repeat that answer. The interpreter didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: By the authorities, from the municipal to the republican authorities, no distinction was made and no discrimination took place along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, you know, you've already said it's not out of the question that they were threatened; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Mind you, you have to look into the specific historical situation. At that time we had 12.500 refugees at Pale. At one point -- or previously the policemen were always in charge of neighbourhoods and knew what was going on. At this point in time, this was not the case anymore. I know that there was some private groups that went around and threatened people. What I'm stating is that this was not the official authorities. I know that even at one meeting of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Coro raised this issue about a man whose name was not mentioned and the representative of the police station said that there were people coming at Pale in uniform from elsewhere and other municipalities. So there could have been cases like that one. What I'm claiming with certainty is that nobody from the Pale police station was responsible for such conduct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, what I'm putting to you is that life for the non-Serbs in Pale - and this Chamber has heard it - life for the non-Serbs was actually a misery. They were harassed and threatened by the Bosnian Serb police. They were harassed and threatened and assaulted by paramilitaries, special units who could do whatever they wanted, but they were known people from the area including Rajko Kusic. They couldn't travel. They had no TV. They had no phone lines. They couldn't even go into some shops. Life for them was a misery, and they had been complaining about it to municipal authorities for months; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: There were complaints made. The municipal authorities tried to help with this as best they could. Throughout the time they were at Pale, we had excellent communication with them. We helped them as far as we were able to. However, I tell you, in a situation where we had 12.000 refugees at Pale and there was the peculiarity, there were refugees from Pofalici, a number of whom had been killed and nobody has been held to account for that, it was impossible to keep things under control. As for the domestic police forces and the domestic population, the local population, I can claim with absolute certainty that conduct on their part was proper and decent. There were even quite touching scenes when these people were leaving Pale. I'm sure that you must have heard about it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence, Mr. Sarac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that when Muslims were leaving Pale, there were moving scenes where their Serbian neighbours were seeing them off, kissing them, saying good-bye, and this is not something when it came to one -- the one side, the second side, or the third side, this is not something that was ever experienced elsewhere in the country.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And in line 20 on previous page, it had been said in Pofalici had been killed up to 300 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You overlapped with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it is now in the transcript. In line 20, the witness said: Refugees from Pofalici where up to 300 Serbs had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in these desperate conditions when republican leader Nikola Koljevic tells the members of the non-Serb community: It doesn't matter what you want, that you want to stay on living here, it doesn't matter what you want, but the Serbs don't want to continue living with you here. That --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: P733, paragraph 38, page 7, pages 12 and 13 in your language, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown this, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps Dr. Karadzic could do this in his re-direct examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- if he would like to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When they get -- when the non-Serbs get told that by a republican leader, living in these desperate conditions, that leaves them with no choice about where they might find safety and security. They have no confidence when the leader tells them that he doesn't want to be living with them anymore, that they're going to be able to live safe and protected, can they? They have no confidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: You saw the letter by the Pale Crisis Staff addressing the Muslims. The Crisis Staff did everything in its power to help these people, to provide them with supplies and everything else. As for the statement by late Professor Koljevic, I really cannot believe that he said this. It's an expressional humanist, a Shakespearologist, who spoke English better than an English lord. I would really like to hear a recording of this statement if it exists. Never in his life did Nikola Koljevic state something like this nor did I ever hear him say this. It could only be hearsay evidence, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe it would be fair if the witness were told who said this or shown it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can show his statement. Yes, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just for a couple of seconds more. Your Honours, your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's fair that the non-Serbs in Pale -- it's fair to say that the non-Serbs in Pale were actually left with no choice about whether they could stay or go, isn't that the case, given all the conditions that you've described and you've agreed to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Mind you, the economic situation was disastrous. Food was in short supply, but whatever there was, was shared around. Most of it went to the refugees as well as to the local population. There was no discrimination on that score, I assure you. That it was nice living in Pale at the time, well, certainly not because in that case we would not have seen as many Serbs leaving the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please wait for the interpretation to end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat. You're delaying it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 8, the witness said it was shared amongst everyone, not shared around. [In English] To everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarac, the non-Serbs didn't have any real choice about where they could stay -- whether they could stay or go, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: You see, the freedom of movement is guaranteed under the constitution. We were aware of the sensitivity of the situation. There were dozens of delegations of Muslims coming and asking that they be allowed to leave to Sarajevo until the situation got stabilised. A Municipal Assembly was held. The meeting lasted the entire day, and ultimately this conclusion that you referred to was issued, which reiterated what the document stated, that the citizens of Muslim and Croat ethnicity who so wished be allowed to change their place of residence in an organised fashion and that the police station should facilitate the implementation of the decision. The majority submitted a request to this effect. Let me just emphasise that it had to do with the change of place of residence, not domicile or permanent residence. Residence is temporary. Domicile is permanent --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarac --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: -- so their place of permanent residence would remain in Pale, whereas their place of residence would be the place of their choosing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like you for a second for this last question to stop taking a legalistic approach and put yourself in the shoes of your non-Serb neighbours and what they were experiencing at the time, because you were there and you saw it and you heard about it and you've talked about it in your statement. You've said how difficult it was. They had no real choice anymore, did they? All they were looking for was safety and security. They had no real choice about whether or not they could stay or go; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: I repeat, in Pale at that point in time it wasn't easy for anyone, for Serbs or Muslims. These people thought that it was the better choice to go to the Federation, and that happened elsewhere too. That is to say that there was no organised action to expel these people, I mean to expel them. They left according to the procedure, about which you have documents. That it was easy for us, no, it wasn't easy for them or for us. The situation was very bad for all citizens of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm done, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much do you need for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I'll be done before 3.00, considerably before 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to change the tape in five minutes and which take about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to continue, we need some break. We better have a break for 15 minutes now and continue for your re-examination, but there are a couple of things I'd like to deal with. First, Mr. Robinson, the Defence's motion for the -- I forgot the name, to request the -- your request that Mr. Jankovic's counsel to be present in the courtroom is granted, Aleksandar Aleksic. And second, the Chamber is seized of the motion -- Defence motion for subpoena to Witness KDZ145 or alternative orders. Mr. Tieger, I know that it is your practice that -- not to respond to the Defence subpoena motion, but given that this motion includes "alternative orders," the Chamber would be assisted to be hearing from you, if you could file it by close of business on Monday. Thank you. That said, we'll continue at 3.00 to conclude this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: For the remainder of this session, we are going to be sitting under Rule 15 bis, due to Judge Kwon's absence for his urgent personal business. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We consulted a bit and we were wondering whether more questions should be put about everything that was read to you, and things that were omitted, but we're giving up and we're just putting two questions to you. Were there any non-Serbs who stayed on in Pale --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I think that's very sensible. I mean, one of the golden rules about re-examination is it's not necessary to get the witness to repeat things that he said in cross-examination. Obviously the object of re-examination is to clarify matters or have explanatory matters, but simple repetition isn't going to really assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency, but the general observation is based on this assertion that non-Serbs had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is whether there were any non-Serbs who chose to stay in Pale during the war?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: All the Pale Croats stayed in Pale. As far as I know, only one Croat woman left, a few Muslims were left there too, and some were even members of the armed forces. I remember, for example, Turkovic was. Also the commander of the garrison in Pale was Anton Sinkovic who was a Croat from Zagorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarac, thank you for having come. Thank you for having testified.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SARAC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Anything arising? Anything further today?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, anything further before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to -- I convinced Dr. Karadzic not to ask the witness about this, but I would just like to put on the record that the citation to the statement of Mr. Koljevic that was made by Ms. Edgerton was to an amalgamated witness statement of Sulejman Cancalo [phoen]. So I thought the impression might have been created that this was some kind of statement which we had a recording of, but that's not the case. So I just thought it was important to point out that without the necessity of putting that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Witness, for coming to The Hague to give your testimony. The Court is grateful to you for your assistance. You're now free to go and a safe journey home, but we will rise all together and the court will be adjourned until 9.00 on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of February, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.06 p.m.,
